info.name: EMC Auth Server
info.description:
# EMC Auth Server — API Collection

Self-hosted multi-tenant Identity Provider. This collection is intended to be run
**top to bottom**: folders are numbered, and later folders depend on values the
earlier ones capture.

## RUN ORDER — read this first

Folders are numbered because **execution order is part of the contract**. Later
folders consume variables that earlier ones capture. Run them top to bottom.

| # | Folder | Needs | Produces |
|---|---|---|---|
| 00 | Smoke | nothing | — |
| 01 | **Bootstrap — run first** | seed admin creds | `access_token`, `refresh_token`, `tenant_id`, `user_id`, `token_kid` |
| 02 | Signing Keys & JWKS (#95) | 01 | `active_kid`, `next_kid`, `jwks_etag` |
| 03 | Auth — Token Flow | 01 | `testUserEmail`, fresh token pair |
| 04 | Applications & M2M | 01 | `client_id`, `client_secret`, `m2m_token`, `application_id` |
| 05 | MFA — TOTP & Email | 01 + **manual `totpCode`** | `totp_secret` |
| 06 | Password & Email | 03 (needs a user) + **manual `reset_token`** | — |
| 07 | Admin — Tenants, Users, Roles | 01 | `new_tenant_id`, `new_tenant_slug` |
| 08 | API Keys & Management Tokens | 01 | `api_key`, `management_token` |
| 09 | Audit Logs | 02 (to have rotation events to find) | — |
| 99 | Negative & Security | 01 | — |

**If you only do one thing:** run `01 · Bootstrap`, then whatever folder you care
about. A 401 anywhere almost always means `01` was skipped or the 15-minute access
token expired — re-run `01`.

Inside a folder, requests are also ordered. `02`'s rotation drill in particular
must run in sequence (prepare → confirm published → complete → verify both sides),
because that sequence *is* the zero-downtime guarantee being tested.

## Adding a new feature — the daily practice

When you add or change an endpoint, do these five things in the same PR:

1. **Put the request in the right numbered folder.** New feature area → new
   numbered folder, inserted where its dependencies allow. Renumber rather than
   append out of order.
2. **Write the description.** Say *why* the endpoint exists and what is
   non-obvious about it (auth required, what it returns only once, what it
   deliberately does not tell the caller). If the description only restates the
   URL, it is not worth having.
3. **Add at least one test.** A request with no assertion is documentation, not a
   test.
4. **Do NOT write a variable setter.** If your endpoint returns something a later
   request needs, add its field name to `CAPTURE_MAP` in the collection-level
   post-response script. One line, and every future endpoint returning that field
   gets it for free.
5. **Add the negative case to `99`.** Especially for anything that is an
   authorization boundary. Happy paths fail loudly; boundaries regress silently.

Then re-export the collection over `postman/EMC-Auth.postman_collection.json` and
commit it with the code change. The JSON is the source of truth — edit in Postman,
export, commit.

## Quick start

1. Import this collection and `EMC-Auth.local.postman_environment.json`.
2. Select the environment; confirm `baseUrl`, `adminEmail`, `adminPassword`.
3. Run **`01 · Bootstrap`** first — it captures the tokens everything else needs.
4. Then run any folder, or the whole collection via the Runner.

## How variables get set (read this before adding requests)

You almost never write a `pm.environment.set` by hand. The **collection-level test
script** (Collection → Scripts → Post-response) auto-captures known fields from
every response — `access_token`, `refresh_token`, `client_id`, `client_secret`,
`api_key`, `kid`, ids, and more — searching the top level plus `data`, `meta`, and
`tokens`.

To make a new field capturable, add one line to `CAPTURE_MAP` in that script.
Do **not** add a per-request setter; that is the pattern this design exists to avoid.

The same script also applies baseline assertions to *every* request: no 5xx,
under 5s, security headers present, no private key material, no `jwt_secret`.
Those run whether or not the request author remembered them.

## Conventions (please keep these)

- **Numbered folders.** Execution order is part of the contract.
- **Every request has a description** explaining *why* it exists, not just what it
  calls. If the only thing to say is the URL, the request is not pulling its weight.
- **Every request has at least one test.** A request with no assertion is
  documentation, not a test.
- **Negative tests live in `99`.** Authorization boundaries are what regress
  silently; happy paths fail loudly on their own.
- **Unique-per-run data.** Use `{{uniqueEmail}}` / `{{uniqueTenant}}` /
  `{{uniqueAppName}}` so a second run is not a 409.
- **Clean up what you create.** Delete at the end of the folder that created it.
- **Secrets stay out of the collection.** Passwords and keys belong in the
  environment, and the environment file in git holds only local dev values.

## Auth

Collection-level Bearer auth uses `{{access_token}}`, so requests inherit it.
Requests that must not use it set `noauth` explicitly (public endpoints, or a
negative test that supplies its own header).

## What needs a human

Three things cannot be automated and say so in their folder description:
TOTP codes (`totpCode`), password-reset tokens (`reset_token`), and the social
login browser redirect. For the dev stack, read emails from Mailpit at
http://localhost:8025.

## CI

```bash
newman run postman/EMC-Auth.postman_collection.json \
  -e postman/EMC-Auth.local.postman_environment.json \
  --folder "00 · Smoke" --folder "01 · Bootstrap — run first" \
  --folder "02 · Signing Keys & JWKS (#95)" --folder "99 · Negative & Security" \
  --reporters cli,junit
```

Folders `00`, `01`, `02`, `99` are safe and fast for CI. The rest create and delete
data, so point them at a disposable database.

// Access tokens are 15 minutes. A run that starts with a stale token fails in
// confusing places, so surface it up front.

Cheapest possible confirmation that the server is up and correctly configured.
Run this first when something looks broken — it separates "server down" from
"my request is wrong" in two seconds.

`emc_auth_legacy_hs256_verifications_total`. It must be flat at zero before

item.name: 02 · Signing Keys & JWKS (#95)
item.description:
Asymmetric signing (issue #95). This folder is the acceptance test for it.

The property being proven: **a third party can verify an EMC token using only
published public keys, and cannot mint one.** Under the old HS256 scheme those
two capabilities were the same capability.

Run in order — the rotation drill depends on the requests above it.

The tenant's public signing keys. Unauthenticated and safe to be — public key
material is not a secret.

Per-tenant by path because keys are per tenant: Acme's public key must not verify
Globex's tokens. The slug lives in the path (not `X-Tenant-Slug`) because a
browser or JWKS library fetching a URL cannot send a custom header.

Give consumers this exact URL. Note it derives from `APP_BASE_URL`, **not** from
the `iss` claim — those are separate settings in this server.

item.name: JWKS from a hostile Origin (must NOT be 403)

request.description:
Regression guard for a specific hazard found during issue #95.

`TenantCORS` is mounted globally, and with a non-empty `GLOBAL_CORS_ORIGINS` it
answers an unknown `Origin` with a hard `403 {"error":"origin not allowed"}`.
For an endpoint whose entire purpose is being fetched by relying parties we have
never heard of, that is wrong — it would make browser-side verification
impossible for every tenant not manually added to a server-wide env var.

JWKS is therefore exempted and serves `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *`.

Revalidation must be cheap. Libraries refetch JWKS whenever they see an unknown
`kid`, so a 304 path is what keeps this endpoint from becoming a hot dependency.

The rate limiter refunds the token for a 304 specifically so well-behaved clients
are not penalised.

Requires "Published JWKS" to have run first (it captures `jwks_etag`).
Unauthenticated endpoints must not confirm which tenants exist. Same 404 for absent and disabled.

Signing-key metadata for the caller's tenant. Requires `tenant:manage`.

Never returns private key material — the response struct has no field for it, so
a handler cannot leak it by accident. The collection-level test asserts this on
every response anyway.

Tenant comes from the JWT, never the request (Non-Negotiable #4), so an operator
cannot inspect another tenant's keys.

Generates the next key and **publishes it in JWKS without signing anything**.

This split is why rotation is zero-downtime. Verifiers cache JWKS, so if a new
key's first token arrived before the key appeared in the published set, every
verifier with a warm cache would reject that token until it refetched.

Idempotent — calling it twice returns the same pending key rather than churning
key material.

item.name: 03 · Auth — Token Flow
item.description:
The core end-user authentication lifecycle: register, login, refresh, inspect,
logout. Uses a per-run unique email so the folder is re-runnable.

request.description:
Creates an end user in the tenant named by `X-Tenant-Slug`.

The slug is **mandatory** here, unlike login. Email is unique per tenant
(`UNIQUE (tenant_id, email)`), so email alone does not identify an account, and
registration has no password to disambiguate with.

Note the absence of a tenant slug: Login fetches every candidate matching the
email across tenants and disambiguates by bcrypt.

Known limitation (CLAUDE.md deferred #17): if the same email+password exists in
two tenants, both match and login fails closed with a generic
`invalid credentials` — correct security, misleading message.

Rotates the pair atomically: the old refresh token is revoked before the new one
is issued, so a replay returns 401.

Refresh tokens are **opaque random strings, not JWTs** — which is why the RS256
migration did not affect them, and why a client that refreshes on 401 recovers
by itself during the Phase 4 cutover.
Rotation must be atomic. A reused refresh token is either theft or a bug; either way it must fail.
The caller's own recent auth events — self-service audit view.
Revokes the refresh token. The access token remains valid until it expires (max 15 min) — it is stateless by design.

item.name: 04 · Applications & M2M
item.description:
Registered applications and the `client_credentials` grant.

`client_secret` is returned **once**, on create and on rotate. The collection
captures it automatically; there is no endpoint that will show it to you again.

request.description: Creates an OAuth client. Capture the `client_secret` now — it is never returned again.

Issues a machine token with `aud=emc-auth-m2m`.

Since issue #84 that audience is enforced per route: an M2M token is **refused**
on user endpoints like `/auth/me`, because its `user_id` is a client id and its
`email` is empty. Use the admin API for machine callers.

item.name: M2M token on a user endpoint (expect 401)

request.description:
Issue #84 regression guard. Before it, a machine token was indistinguishable from
a user token and this returned 200 for a caller with no user identity.
Issues a new secret and invalidates the old one. The response is the only place the new secret appears.
Per-application throttle (default 60/min). Note there is currently no tenant-wide cap (CLAUDE.md deferred #13).

item.name: 05 · MFA — TOTP & Email
item.description:
Self-service MFA for the authenticated caller.

**Manual step required.** TOTP activation needs a real 6-digit code from an
authenticator app, which Postman cannot generate. Run Enroll, scan the
`otpauth_url` (or paste `totp_secret` into any TOTP app), then fill `totpCode` in
the environment before running Activate.

request.description: All-method MFA state plus remaining backup codes. Safe to call any time.

Returns the shared secret, an `otpauth://` URL for QR display, and 8 single-use
backup codes.

Secrets are AES-256-GCM encrypted at rest, and backup codes are stored only as
SHA-256 hashes. **This response is the only time you see either in the clear.**

request.description: Confirms enrollment with a live code. Set `totpCode` in the environment first — it cannot be automated.

request.description: Issues a fresh set of 8 and invalidates the previous set. The TOTP secret is unchanged.
Removes the TOTP factor. Blocked when policy makes it the last remaining factor under a 'required' MFA policy.

item.description:
Reset and verification flows.

Both are **deliberately unobservable from the outside**: `/forgot-password`
always returns 200 with an identical body whether or not the email exists

email — read it from Mailpit at http://localhost:8025 in the dev stack.

item.description:
Administrative CRUD. Requires `tenant:manage` (tenants, system views) or

`tenant_id` always comes from the JWT for the caller's own tenant. The

super_admin only (`tenant:manage`). A tenant admin gets 403 here — that is the isolation boundary working.

Creates a tenant, its default permissions, an owner role, and an owner user with a

Since issue #95 it also mints the tenant's RSA signing key pair, so its JWKS

key is generated lazily on first token instead.

item.description:
Long-lived API keys and the short-lived management tokens they exchange for —
EMC's equivalent of an Auth0 management token.

The raw key (`emck_…`) is shown **once**. Only its SHA-256 hash is stored.

request.description:
Trades an API key for a 15-minute JWT with `aud=emc-auth-management`.

Short-lived by design: callers re-exchange rather than holding a long-lived
bearer token. Since #84 that audience is accepted only where an API-key
integration is a legitimate caller.
Cleanup. Revocation is immediate.

item.description:
Audit trail. Writes are fire-and-forget (ADR-09) — an audit failure must never
block an auth operation — so a very recent event may take a moment to appear.

Confirms the #95 rotation endpoints leave an audit trail. Key rotation is a

item.name: 10 - App-Scoped /auth/apps/me (#96)
item.description:
Issue #96 - the app_id claim enforced as an authorization boundary.

Run in order: the setup requests create two applications in one tenant and a user inside application A. The request that matters is 'CROSS-APPLICATION' - everything else is scaffolding or a fail-closed guard.

Requires folder 01 (admin token) and, for the last check, folder 04 (m2m token).

request.description: Application A. Two applications in the SAME tenant are what make the cross-application test meaningful: same signing key, same audience, same tenant - only the app_id claim differs.
Application B. Two applications in the SAME tenant are what make the cross-application test meaningful: same signing key, same audience, same tenant - only the app_id claim differs.

item.name: Setup - register a user inside application A

item.name: Setup - log in through application A

request.description: Yields an app-scoped end-user token whose app_id claim names application A.
Token's app_id matches the calling application, so the request succeeds and returns the SAME payload shape /auth/me returns - consumers change a URL and a header, not their response handling.

item.name: CROSS-APPLICATION - app A token + app B credentials (expect 401)

request.description:
*** THE test for issue #96. ***

Application B presents application A's user token. Same tenant, same signing key, valid signature, correct audience - everything verifies. Only the app_id claim distinguishes them, and before #96 the server ignored it, so this returned 200 and B could read A's users.

If this returns 200, app scoping is NOT working.
Fails closed. Without X-Client-Authorization the server has nothing to compare app_id against, so it must refuse rather than fall back to /auth/me behaviour.
Admin/console tokens carry an empty app_id by design. An empty claim must fail closed here - 'no application' is not 'any application' - even though this same token works fine on /auth/me.

exec: pm.test('status 401 - empty app_id fails closed', () => pm.response.to.have.status(401));

Where #84 and #96 compose. This route sits behind JWTRenew, which pins verification to aud=emc-auth-api, so an emc-auth-m2m token is rejected on AUDIENCE before app scoping is even evaluated.

item.name: 11 · Per-Tenant OIDC Issuer (#7)
item.description:
Issue #7 step 1–3: the `iss` claim moves from one global `JWT_ISSUER` to a
per-tenant `{OIDC_ISSUER_BASE_URL}/tenants/{slug}`.

**Why it matters:** OIDC clients derive the discovery document — and from it
the `jwks_uri` — from the token's own `iss`. With a global issuer that chain
could only ever name one key set, but keys are per-tenant since #95, so no
single URL could verify every tenant's tokens.

**Run 01 · Bootstrap first.** Requests 4 and 5 additionally need 08 · API Keys
and 07 · Admin respectively; both skip themselves cleanly if those have not run.

**The server must be rebuilt** — a container still running the pre-#7 binary
will mint the old global issuer and every assertion here will fail.

item.name: 1 · Login — token carries the per-tenant issuer

request.description:
The core assertion of #7. `iss` must now be
`{{baseUrl}}/tenants/{{tenantSlug}}`, not the old global `JWT_ISSUER`.

Captures `token_iss` for the next request, which rebuilds the JWKS URL
from it exactly as a standards-compliant client would.

`SignManagement` builds its own `RegisteredClaims` literal, separate from

item.name: 8 - CRITICAL: login-code endpoint must refuse an authorization code

request.description:
THE trap that migration 00067 exists to close.

oauth_authorization_codes holds two different credentials. A login_code
(the social-login hand-back) is redeemable at /auth/oauth/exchange with

item.name: 99 · Negative & Security
item.description:
Assertions about what must **fail**. These are the tests that catch a regression
in an authorization boundary — the kind of bug that never shows up in a happy-path
run because everything still returns 200.

Expect red here only when something is genuinely wrong.

request.description: Baseline: a protected route without credentials must refuse.
Malformed input must be refused cleanly, not 500.

The classic JWT attack: an unsigned token claiming `super_admin`.

This server pins the algorithm in **two** independent places — the parser's
`WithValidMethods` option and the keyfunc's own method check — so relaxing one
does not open the hole. `alg: none` is in neither list.

Every query uses pgx positional parameters (Non-Negotiable #2), so this is
credential-checked like any other wrong input. A 500 would mean the payload
reached the planner.

Login is limited to 5/min/IP. Run this request 6+ times (or let the Runner
iterate) to see a 429 with `Retry-After`.

A single execution normally returns 401 — that is not a failure.
